How Do LiLiCorr and Dory Trade Extra Compute for Faster Tokens and Deeper Reasoning?

Even if a single forward pass is fast, generating a 400-token response requires 400 back-to-back forward passes. Speculative decoding breaks that serial chain by using a tiny, fast “drafter” model to guess several future tokens at once, then letting the big target model verify the whole batch in a single parallel pass. Spec Decoding relies on the assumption that, on average, a good portion of the draft model’s speculations are correct. This means that a good portion of the inference is done by a much smaller and cheaper model. Instead of paying for k target model passes, we pay for 1 target model pass and k (much cheaper) draft model passes. Since the draft model is significantly smaller and faster, the overall cost per generated token is substantially reduced.

There is an interesting dilemna with Spec Decoding:

  • If the drafter predicts tokens sequentially, drafting itself becomes slow.

  • If the drafter predicts multiple future positions in parallel, it runs fast — but because each position is guessed independently, the words often clash with each other. For example, imagine that position t+1 assigns high probability to both dog and cat, while position t+2 assigns high probability to both barks and meows. A parallel drafter picking the top token at each slot independently can easily output dog meows — a nonsensical pair that the target model immediately rejects, wasting the draft.

LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding — NVIDIA Nemotron fixes parallel incoherence without going back to slow step-by-step neural drafting. Instead of picking one winner at each draft position right away, LiLiCorr keeps a small shortlist of top candidate tokens at every position, forming a candidate lattice. Next, a tiny two-layer Transformer sweeps across that entire lattice in a single parallel pass. Each candidate token gets a representation enriched by its neighbors in the lattice, the drafter’s confidence, and the target model’s last verified hidden state. That single pass outputs compatibility vectors for every candidate, allowing the system to score how well neighboring words fit together in parallel, followed by a dirt-cheap sequential pass over those precomputed numbers to pick the best path.

On Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, a 1.13-billion-parameter LiLiCorr drafter (excluding shared embeddings and output head) proposing 7 tokens at a time averages 4.68 accepted tokens under greedy decoding and 4.25 under probabilistic sampling — a massive latency win when serving interactive users at low concurrency.

While LiLiCorr spends a bit of extra compute horizontally to draft future tokens faster, Nemotron Labs Dory 1.0 spends extra compute vertically to make a small model punch above its weight class. Dory is a 4-billion-parameter NVFP4 model built with input layers, a shared recurrent middle block, and output layers. Instead of passing through the middle layers once, Dory can loop the same hidden state through that shared block multiple times before emitting a token.

Why loop a 4B model instead of just loading a 12B model? Looping lets you keep a tiny 4B footprint in memory while you can unlock a lot of the intelligence in small models by exploring their internal representations better (which perfectly aligns with our latent space reasoning thesis that most models don’t fail due to a lack of intelligence but from inadequate exploration of their internal representations, more details here)

Notice that going from 1 loop to 2 loops adds over 9 points on SWE-bench Verified and 7.6 points on SciCode, while doubling to 4 loops hits diminishing returns on those two benchmarks (though Terminal-Bench 2.1 keeps climbing from 18.1% to 22.2%). To keep 4 loops from taking 4x the KV cache memory, Dory uses last-loop KV caching, overwriting the recurrent block’s cached states on each pass so memory stays completely flat.

Now step back and look at what happens when you take these fast, compressed models and deploy them across a thousand GPUs in a production data center. Even the most efficient model checkpoint will bleed money if the cluster software schedules it poorly.

Dynamo: Getting More Out of Existing GPUs

Even the fastest GPUs waste money when workloads are poorly scheduled. LLM inference has two very different phases: prefill, which processes prompts in parallel and is compute-intensive, and decode, which generates tokens sequentially and is largely constrained by memory bandwidth. Running both on the same GPUs creates unnecessary contention. NVIDIA’s Dynamo separates these workloads into specialized GPU pools, uses NIXL to transfer KV caches between them, and routes requests toward machines that already hold relevant context. This becomes particularly valuable for AI agents making dozens of tool calls, where repeatedly processing the same conversation history wastes substantial compute.

Thanks to their optimizations NVIDIA reports up to 4x faster time-to-first-token and 1.5x greater throughput in agentic workloads. Combined with TensorRT-LLM’s kernel-level optimizations, Dynamo effectively increases the useful capacity of existing GPU clusters without requiring more hardware.

Once Dynamo and TensorRT-LLM squeeze the software bubbles out of the cluster, you hit the hard physical limits of the hardware itself: how fast wires can move activations between chips, and how many megawatts of electricity the local utility will let you pull from the grid. This is where our final optimization comes in.

Why Is NVIDIA Pairing Vera Rubin GPUs with Groq 3 LPX Accelerators?

Vera Rubin takes this system-level optimization into hardware. Its NVL72 rack connects 72 GPUs through NVLink 6, delivering up to 3.6 TB/s of GPU-to-GPU bandwidth to reduce communication bottlenecks in large Mixture-of-Experts models. Rack-level power smoothing also helps operators use more of their available electrical capacity.

NVIDIA reports roughly 10x higher DeepSeek-R1 inference throughput per megawatt than Grace Blackwell, although this doesn’t translate directly into a 10x reduction in total costs. The more interesting development is its integration with Groq 3 LPX, a specialized accelerator system offering 128GB of on-chip SRAM and 40 PB/s of aggregate bandwidth. Rather than forcing GPUs to handle everything, NVIDIA proposes using Rubin for compute-intensive prefill and attention, while Groq handles latency-sensitive feed-forward and expert operations. The combined architecture reportedly delivers up to 35x higher throughput per megawatt than GB200 NVL72 under NVIDIA’s benchmark conditions. The strategic implication is more important than the benchmark: NVIDIA is preparing for a world where GPUs aren’t necessarily the best processors for every inference operation. By supplying the interconnect, specialized hardware, and orchestration software, it can retain control of the computing system even as workloads become increasingly heterogeneous.

There are several other engineering optimizations they make to really drive down the cost of intelligence, but those are lot more serving/topic specific (or are just not that major/novel), so I don’t think we should spend a lot of time covering them. Instead, we must now take all of this is a setup for the question that most of you are likely here for: why should any of this actually make NVIDIA more money?

When Does Making AI Cheaper Actually Make NVIDIA Richer?

Whenever you ask bulls this question, they immediately point to Jevons Paradox: Make a resource cheaper, people use way more of it (and find completely new uses for it), and thus the total spending goes up around the new industries that spawned out of this new prosperity.

I think that before we really get into the whole AI buildout discussion, it’s important to study a bit of history and see why infrastructure operators bet the farm on that dynamic. When we study how heavy infrastructure (think railroads, fiber-optic networks, and hopefully AI data centers) have made money in the past, a surprisingly consistent pattern emerges — 

In the beginning your capital heavy investment (say railway system) is used by a few people. This means that every individual person has to also carry the cost of paying for the RnD, building, operations etc. To keep trains profitable, you might have to pay 100 USD on a 99 USD cost, giving the railway line a measly 1% margin. At this cost, people would rather Uber or drive.

Now imagine that the government drops the cost by 10x to promote more train usage. This isn’t the financial suicide it seems like on the surface:

  • First, fixed-cost amortization across elastic volume: Because tickets are 10x cheaper, people use the rails for everyday trips they never took at $100. So instead of growing 10x, your volume might grow by 15x (pushing top-line revenue from $100 to $150) while also spreading your fixed infrastructure (railway lines, ticketing systems, train cars etc, all of which would be very expensive one time payments) and customer-acquisition costs across 15x more rides.

  • Second, scale-driven systems innovation: Running at 15x volume exposes every inefficiency in your operations and forces you to innovate on the underlying plumbing (the exact role of LatentMoE, NVFP4, and Dynamo; this research would not have been worth it in a world that wasn’t processing hundreds of trillions of tokens regularly).

Between high utilization and engineering optimizations, your fully loaded cost per unit craters from $99/head down to $7/head. This means that your profits go up 45x (15x usage spike * 3x profit per head), even though your price 10x.

Tie this back to Nvidia and the parrallel becomes clear: crater the cost of intelligence (optimizations), ensure that the intelligence flows through your system (the CUDA ecosystem; in our rail example, worth noting that it’s not the train track maker that profits from Jevons, it’s the railways ), and you will ensure a long lasting dynasty.

So is that all? Not quite. To assume that this play will work out for Nvidia, 3 things have to go right: customers will have to spend more total dollars on AI, this spending will require net-new computing hardware, and that NVIDIA will be the one cashing the hardware checks.

Depending on which of those three links holds or breaks, we get three very different futures (all of which can play out simultaneously across different parts of the market):

  1. NVIDIA creates new demand and captures the value: Cheaper inference unlocks high-value applications, customers buy more compute, and NVIDIA keeps its crown as the default infrastructure supplier of an expanded empire.

  2. NVIDIA creates the demand, but someone else captures the margin: AI usage explodes, but custom hyperscaler ASICs, alternative accelerators, and cloud landlords pocket a growing share of the industry’s profit pool.

  3. NVIDIA creates demand, but efficiency compounds even faster: The increased demand isn’t enough to offset the falling costs, essentially dropping profit margins.

For the rest of this article, we will study the three outcomes which ones might play out (in what contexts since all 3 can happen at once in different degrees and different subspaces) to help us identify where the market is headed and how we can ahead of.

Outcome 1: NVIDIA Creates New Demand and Captures the Value

One of the biggest mistakes analysts make when modeling cheaper inference is assuming all AI workloads have the same price elasticity. In reality, enterprise AI splits into two completely different economic buckets:

  • Capped-value workloads (like a customer-support chatbot): Once a bot is smart enough to resolve routine refund tickets, making the model twice as smart doesn’t justify spending twice as much. When inference gets 50% cheaper, the enterprise simply pockets the savings and moves on.

  • Uncapped-value workloads (like an autonomous coding agent): Give a coding agent 10x more test-time compute to inspect repository dependencies, draft candidate patches, run unit tests, and verify its own pull requests, and it starts solving engineering tickets it previously failed on. Here, extra tokens aren’t an overhead cost; they directly manufacture higher-value labor.

Given the conversations around Swarms breaking into systems, I think we might even see a future subgroup of uncapped workloads, which essentially operate on the insurance model — did you really invest resources into checking for vulnerabilities in your base, with certification agencies for the security measures conducted (so even if you get hacked, insurance would cover you). The reason I’m calling this out differently is because unlike standard uncapped value workloads (which are economically beneficial), these are more insurance/downside protection coded ( can you really afford to get hacked and possibly lose billions from reputational loss; and if you do get hacked wouldn’t you want to be able to say that you did what was industry best so you’re not completely ruined by bad PR). In a way, this kind of growth would be the AI industry monetizing a problem it helped create (although I’m sure some will argue that the problem was the human written bugs from older times).

We don’t have to guess whether these uncapped workloads are driving real hardware demand; Anthropic’s November S-1 amendment gives us the receipts:

  • In the first nine months of 2026, enterprise demand for coding and agentic workflows pushed Anthropic’s revenue up 13x to 33.24 billion USD (driven by 11,900+ enterprises spending over 100K USD a year, including 250 whales spending over 10M USD).

  • To feed that usage, Anthropic had to grow its compute bill 4.3x to 18.81 billion USD. In fact, demand outran their contracted clusters so badly in Q3 that Anthropic had to drop 5 billion USD on overpriced, short-term spot compute just to keep the lights on (temporarily swinging them from a 974M USD Q2 operating profit to a 567M USD Q3 loss).

At one level, Ant eating that 5 Billion Penalty to get energized racks online ASAP is a HUGE positive signal. However, there is a less flattering alternative interpretation here. Because Anthropic’s revenue grew 13x while its compute bill only grew 4.3x, the revenue Anthropic extracts from every dollar of compute jumped from 0.58 USD to 1.77 USD (even with training and R&D baked in). When NVIDIA’s engineering makes clusters more productive during a hardware shortage, model providers and clouds don’t hand 100% of that efficiency back to NVIDIA in new chip orders — they keep prices steady and pocket a big slice of the efficiency delta as their own margin expansion.

Now here, one might argue that Nvidia’s ecosystem that lets it engineer efficiency at scale will create a premium for Nvidia products in the short term, similar to their existing premium in Cuda, but I think the overall trend is toward customers pocketing efficiency gains, simply b/ of the value chain involved and how far back Nvidia has to sit:

Useful AI work → Customer spending → Net-new infrastructure required → NVIDIA’s share of hardware orders → NVIDIA’s gross profit

Once Anthropic and its 11,900 enterprise accounts (who generate 74% of its revenue) stare at an 18.81 billion USD annual compute bill, their number one financial priority becomes breaking that fourth link in the chain — which brings us directly to Outcome 2.

Outcome 2: NVIDIA Creates the Market, but Someone Else Gets the Money

Every billion dollars a hyperscaler or frontier lab sends to Santa Clara gives them another billion reasons to build an escape hatch ( even Anthropic, which has historically only been laser focused on models and crying wolf to not have to compete against open models, explictly laid out a 4-hardware plan across NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, and AMD accelerators to maximize their intelligence per dollar).

Unfortunately, this investment in cost reduction, might not trickle down to the customers. When it comes down to it, if a model/agent company can drop their costs of intelligence 10x, what stops them from keeping the margins for themselves. Especially in a world where competitors will not undercut them (compute is constrained, so there is an upper limit to the amount of demand you can capture there). Too see this phenomenon in action, let’s take a look at some of the research done by the Gs at SemiAnalysis and their breakdown of the cost of Google’s TPU v7 — 

Developing the chip internally costs Google roughly 1.03 USD per chip-hour (or 1.21 USD on an external ownership basis), which Google then rents out on Google Cloud for ~2.00 USD per chip-hour on a three-year commitment. Google can essentially price just below the GPU rental cost, drive demand to themselves, and pocket the margins for themselves.

So why hasn’t everyone dumped NVIDIA for cheaper ASICs already? This is where Nvidia’s software ecosystem becomes clutch. Thanks to the ubiquity of CUDA and Nvidia GPUs, a lot of effort has been invested in improving the utilization of Nvidia’s hardware (both by internal and external folk), which lets them overcome the raw hardware differences. This is shown very clearly in the October SemiAnalysis InferenceX benchmarks on Qwen3.5 (at 200 tok/s/user):

  • On a pure hardware basis (both chips running standard FP8): Google’s cheaper TPU v7 beats NVIDIA’s GB300 NVL72 by 1.85x in tokens per dollar.

  • With NVIDIA’s full-stack optimizations turned on (NVFP4 + Dynamo + TensorRT-LLM): Because TPU v7 lacks native four-bit arithmetic, cutting the byte payload in half lets GB300 flip the scoreboard and beat TPU v7 by 1.84x in tokens per dollar (assuming your workload tolerates any unmeasured quality gap between FP4 and FP8; this is also why we spent so much time understanding the engineering efforts Nvidia is taking to keep intelligence high at much lower costs).

This inversion when software comes into play means that NVIDIA it’s relatively protected from costly wars of attrition, since it wins on quality, not cheaper bare metal. This has let them keep the margins for now, even as the ASIC boys have spawned off a whole zoo of competitors, and why I think that too much money is invested in chip designs and not enough in reshaping the ecosystem around it.

Back to Nvidia, this inversion and software moat does have it’s own kinds of risks however. Generally speaking software is easier to produce than hardware (especially as agents produce more and more of it), and unlike previous times, heavy weights have a massive incentive to attack the said moats. This means that Nvidia is in a perpetual arms race to keep their software ahead of the curve. We’re already seeing this in real time as Google’s next inference chip, TPU 8i, adds native FP4 support, erasing that specific advantage, which forces NVIDIA to invent the next system primitive (like Rubin + Groq LPX disaggregation) just to protect its pricing power.

Assuming worst case here, what happens if hyperscalers eventually close that systems gap? This leaves Nvidia with 3 options:

  • Taxing competitor racks (NVLink Fusion): By letting third-party chipmakers plug into NVIDIA’s rack fabric (cc it’s deal with Rebellions into NVLink Fusion for SK Telecom )NVIDIA can still sell switches and NICs when it loses the GPU socket. This will unfortunately be a pure volume play since networking plumbing doesn’t replace 75% flagship GPU margins. They will also lose some major customers since Google and AWS use their own proprietary fabrics anyway.

  • Charging for enterprise software: NVIDIA AI Enterprise lists at 4,500 USD per GPU per year (plus commercial NIM licensing). There is a huge market to address with enterprise software, and Nvidia’s brands will make it a preferred provider compared to the many other software grunts and new gen Palantir’s teeming in the market. However, to replace just 40 billion USD of annual hardware gross profit at an illustrative 90% software margin, NVIDIA would need nearly 10 million GPUs paying full list price (or ~20 million GPUs at a 50% paid attach rate before discounts).

  • Selling turnkey Sovereign AI factories: National buildouts in Japan and Korea love NVIDIA’s integrated racks and free open-weight models b/c governments lack internal ASIC teams. This can be a huge long term play as sovereign countries will want their ai to be protected in their own controls (so that they aren’t reliant on another countries policies; look at what happened when Fable was banned in other countries), but this will be a much longer buildout, and there is a chance that the other countries will eventually want to move their supply chain dependency off Nvidia onto local manufacturers.

Putting all this together tells us that whether Nvidia capturing margins, instead of becoming one of many, ultimately boils down to whether they can keep their full stack efficiency higher than everyone else. I parallel it almost to higher education — in an ecosystem teeming with colleges and online certifications, a Harvard/Stanford degree becomes more valuable since it acts as a signal (regardless whether it works or not). Similarly, as long as Nvidia keeps a strong full stack lead, I think the fragmentation in the AI hardware market will cause decision paralysis and make companies instinctively reach for Nvidia (even if there is a premium).

With all this discussed, let’s look at the weirdest risk of all: what happens if NVIDIA’s engineers are too good at their jobs?

Outcome 3: NVIDIA Creates Demand, but Efficiency Improves Even Faster

When a cloud provider installs Dynamo, switches to NVFP4, and makes its existing GPU cluster 30% more productive in the middle of a compute shortage, everybody celebrates. Waiting customers immediately soak up the extra capacity, and the cloud provider still buys every new GPU it can find.

Run that exact same 30% software upgrade when the cluster already has enough capacity to serve paying customers, however, and the math flips. Instead of buying more racks, the cloud provider just delays its next hardware order.

If effective compute supply starts growing faster than paying demand, NVIDIA runs into a competitor that is much harder to beat than AMD or Google: the millions of GPUs NVIDIA already sold two years ago (a brand-new Rubin rack has to generate enough revenue to pay back tens of thousands of dollars in fresh capital expenditure, while a depreciated H100 sitting in an already-wired rack only has to cover electricity, cooling, and basic maintenance to stay cash-flow positive +every time NVIDIA ships a free software update that speeds up inference, that paid-off H100 gets more productive for free).

We haven’t hit that saturation point yet. Silicon Data’s H100 rental index tells us that even the ancient H100s rent at around 3–3.1 USD per GPU-hour. As older fleets pay off their upfront capex, the productivity hurdle NVIDIA’s newest chips have to clear just to justify rip-and-replace upgrades gets steeper every year.

There’s another overlooked wrinkle that makes this analysis messy: software moves on internet time, while the electrical grid moves on utility time (this is also why so many neoclouds are hitting credit crunches, since their investors anchored their expectations to software lifecyccles (they were tech investors), and completely overlooked that the short-medium term constraints would all be blocked by physical problems that the tech industry had never dealt with, due to which growth hasn’t been as smooth as anticipated).

This means that while you can drop a 2x model optimization overnight, you can’t summon high-voltage transformers or substation hookups on command (the IEA estimates grid bottlenecks could delay roughly 20% of planned data-center capacity through 2030). That physical bottleneck pulls operators in two completely opposite directions depending on their balance sheet:

  • If you already own an energized building with a fixed megawatt cap: Power efficiency is king. Swapping older GPUs for Rubin racks that squeeze 10x more tokens out of the same electrical allocation lets you serve way more customers without waiting three years for the utility company — assuming you have paying customers lined up for those extra tokens.

  • If you are borrowing billions to build new sites from scratch: NVIDIA’s frantic annual hardware cycle and power delays put you in a brutal vise. Look at CoreWeave’s Q2 2026 numbers: the company brought in 2.575 billion USD in quarterly revenue, paid 640 million USD in net interest, and watched 1.393 billion USD (54% of its entire top-line revenue) vanish straight into depreciation and amortization — all while waiting on 748MW of undelivered power across two leased site groups phasing in through 2028.

Pause on that 54% depreciation number for a second. When more than half of your revenue goes toward hardware losing value on the shelf, timing can kill you. Buy GPUs too early before your power is hooked up, and NVIDIA launches a 2x faster architecture before your chips earn their first dollar; wait until the substation is live, and you risk hardware shortages or blown customer deadlines.

This is where NVIDIA’s incentives clash directly with its infrastructure partners: NVIDIA wants to make its own hardware obsolete every 12 months to force new purchases, while its debt-financed cloud customers desperately need older generations to stay economically relevant long enough to pay back their lenders (this is also why Coreweave and co have very generous depreciation schedules).

In 2027, that timing gamble will reach a boiling point. SemiAnalysis forecasts a massive wave of delayed data-center shells finally coming online in 2027 — 

If empty buildings suddenly outpace chip supply — especially with the IEA’s November 2026 analysis projecting high-bandwidth memory (HBM) shortages through at least the end of 2027 — the bottleneck swings from power right back to silicon. NVIDIA has already positioned its balance sheet for that exact flip, locking in roughly 279 billion USD in supply and manufacturing commitments (per its latest 10-Q) so it controls the memory and packaging when customers finally have rooms ready to fill.

But what happens if all those new 2027 buildings come online at the exact same time as 10x hardware jumps, 3.5x LatentMoE gains, and 4x Dynamo scheduling speedups? Effective computing capacity could multiply far faster than raw megawatts or GPU shipment counts suggest — even while total token usage keeps climbing.

And if effective supply overshoots paying demand, NVIDIA can’t simply tee hee and walk away, because it has been using its own balance sheet to finance the buildout. In August, NVIDIA agreed to provide up to 105 billion USD in contingent guarantees (disclosed in its 10-Q) backing land, power, and building shells for OpenAI-linked infrastructure in Ohio, phasing in starting fiscal 2029.

On one hand, guaranteeing 20-year power shells is a smart strategic play:

  • Securing the Ohio campus locks in sockets for several future generations of NVIDIA racks.

  • Funding independent neoclouds expands NVIDIAs customer base so it isn’t held hostage by three hyperscalers.

But at the same time, it’s undeniable that those neoclouds are currently pass-through landlords leasing compute back to the exact same handful of frontier labs (like Anthropic, which carries roughly 895 billion USD in multi-year compute commitments across hardware suppliers, with 69.8 billion USD due in the next 12 months). So Nvidia is still left to deal with the reality that while they can help finance their customers’ infrastructure to speed up adoption, this will only work until their end-user revenue fails to cover the rent. This is another reason why Nvidia is so frantic about market expansion, since the Neoclouds it’s investing into can only survive if they see a lot of customer growth outside of the valley.

Where Does All of This Leave Us?

The biggest takeaway from studying NVIDIA’s engineering alongside its balance sheet is that “AI demand” and “GPU demand” are no longer the same line on a chart. Every optimization we covered in Part 1 drives a wedge between the two, meaning AI usage can 10x from here while hardware profits go through a massive regime shift.

If I had to bet on how our three outcomes play out, they won’t happen as separate timelines — they’ll split the market in two:

  • Routine, capped-value AI (basic enterprise workflows, standard RAG, customer support) will slide rapidly into Outcomes 2 and 3. Once a workload stabilizes, hyperscaler ASICs and paid-off H100s are more than good enough to run it, squeezing NVIDIA out of the commodity tier.

  • Frontier, uncapped-value AI (autonomous coding, continuous cyber-defense swarms, physical robotics) will stay locked in Outcome 1, because those workloads are so compute-starved that they need NVIDIA’s bleeding-edge system tricks just to be economically viable.

In other words, NVIDIA is quietly trading away the commodity floor of the AI market to keep a monopoly on the ceiling. Whether that trade makes NVIDIA richer over the next 24 months comes down to three signals I’ll be tracking:

  1. Enterprise cohort graduation: Are 100K USD customer accounts graduating into the 1M+ USD tier fast enough to pay off the industry’s nearly 1 trillion USD in forward compute commitments?

  2. Real-world ASIC software parity: How quickly do chips like TPU 8i close the production TCO gap once NVIDIA’s software lead is factored in?

  3. Used H100 rental rates in 2027: When the delayed wave of 2027 data-center power finally flips on, spot rental prices on depreciated GPUs will be the first canary in the coal mine telling us if software efficiency has finally outrun paying demand.

articles.title: What MaintainX’s $3.6 billion acquisition tells us about industrial AI and the value of solving boring problems.
articles.content:
In Silicon Valley, we’re talking about autonomous agents, world models, robotics, and machines that might eventually reason about the physical world. Meanwhile, many factories are still trying to get their maintenance teams off spreadsheets.
And there’s a surprisingly large business in fixing that.
I recently spoke with Nick Haase, co-founder of MaintainX, a company that builds software for the people maintaining factories, machines, and other physical infrastructure. MaintainX now serves roughly 15,000 organizations, according to Nick, and was acquired by Autodesk for approximately $3.6 billion in August 2026.
What interested me wasn’t simply the acquisition. It was how much of MaintainX’s success came from recognizing problems that look almost embarrassingly simple to someone working in modern software.
Factories are full of expensive machines, highly skilled workers, and sophisticated engineering. Yet much of the information needed to operate those machines is scattered across incompatible software, paper records, and the memories of people who have been doing the job for decades. As AI becomes increasingly capable, that gap is becoming more important. The opportunity isn’t necessarily to introduce the most advanced technology into a factory. It’s to understand why the factory isn’t already working as efficiently as it should, then figure out which parts of that problem technology can actually solve.
Recently, I came across an article called Robotics' New Era After Astra by and it had one of the most surprising learnings I’ve read recently— “On September 4, RoboCurve published a simple experiment: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra controlled two robotic arms and was asked to pick up a block and place it into a bowl. It succeeded in 19 out of 20 trials. A month later, NVIDIA’s Astranomy study tested Astra across 120 simulated manipulation tasks. Its best configuration achieved a 74.8% success rate, significantly outperforming several specialized robotics models on the same benchmark.
The surprising part? Astra was not designed as a robotics foundation model. A general-purpose model trained on reasoning, vision, coding, and tool use can now perform meaningful physical tasks without task-specific robot-policy fine-tuning.”
I get a lot of questions about robotics and physical AI, and while I find the space interesting, I’m not an expert. I found this article to be an exceptional primer to this topic, with a great seeding for my further exploration. If you’re looking to learn more about all of this, this will be a great place to start.

Nick estimates that maintenance technicians spend only 25–35% of their time actually working on equipment. The rest goes toward finding information, paperwork, coordination, and other tasks.
A big reason is accumulated software and processes. Companies introduce new systems without retiring old ones, leaving workers to manage information across multiple platforms.
Manufacturing is also relatively risk-averse, often for good reason. A failed software implementation can disrupt production and cost substantial money.
Many facilities still rely heavily on spreadsheets, whiteboards, and paper. Even reliable connectivity and mobile devices aren’t universal.
Factories already generate large amounts of machine and sensor data. What they often lack is the context needed to interpret it.
Maintenance history, technician observations, equipment failures, and operational decisions frequently aren’t connected to that data.
This is also a workforce problem. Experienced technicians are retiring, taking years of undocumented knowledge with them.
Nick’s view is that the manufacturers that learn to capture and use this knowledge will have a substantial advantage. More sophisticated AI won’t accomplish much if the underlying information is unreliable.
MaintainX didn’t begin by selling exclusively to large manufacturers. Some of its earliest customers were country clubs, car washes, and fast-food franchises.
The company offered a free product and made it easy for smaller businesses to adopt its software.
That helped in several ways:
Smaller businesses had fewer procurement barriers and could adopt products faster.
Their feedback helped MaintainX improve its product.
The company discovered that maintenance problems were surprisingly similar across very different industries.
It could establish a customer base and credibility before pursuing major enterprise contracts.
Nick mentioned that some enterprise RFPs still ask whether a company has existed for at least ten years. Building trust takes time, and smaller customers can help bridge that gap.
We discussed the distinction between improving efficiency and expanding markets.
For a manufacturer operating at capacity, increasing production might normally require building another factory.
But if better maintenance and operations can increase throughput using existing equipment, the company can serve additional demand without that capital expenditure.
Nick also mentioned factories holding tens of millions of dollars in spare-parts inventory without adequate visibility into what they own.
These are opportunities to improve working capital, increase production, and make better use of existing assets.
I shared an experience working with a manufacturer on feasibility assessments for incoming customer orders.
Our initial instinct was to use a complex multi-agent system. But that created too much complexity for the users.
A simpler approach worked better: present the assumptions, explain the reasoning, and let the user question and refine the assessment.
Nick made a similar point about introducing AI to factory workers. Sometimes it’s better not to present a feature as AI at all. Just make it useful and understandable.
One interesting aspect of Autodesk’s acquisition of MaintainX is the potential to connect equipment design with actual operational performance.
Information about how machines fail, how they’re repaired, and how they perform in production could eventually inform future engineering decisions.
This creates a feedback loop between designing equipment and understanding how it behaves in the real world.
It’s also an example of why companies that capture useful operational data can become strategically valuable.
Nick’s advice was remarkably practical: visit factories.
Call manufacturers, speak with production managers, attend regional trade shows, and ask to observe operations.
Don’t start by asking people what software they want. Ask what their day looks like, where they lose time, and which parts of their work are frustrating.
For someone early in their career, he even suggested spending a year working inside a manufacturing company and building internal tools.
His broader advice was to focus on solving one specific problem exceptionally well rather than trying to automate everything.
Nick sees opportunities in material science, process simulation, equipment optimization, and predictive maintenance.
But much of the immediate opportunity is less complicated: improving basic information systems, reducing administrative work, and helping manufacturers make better decisions with the equipment and data they already have.
A recurring theme throughout our conversation was that technical capability and practical judgment are different things. AI is making it much easier to build software, but knowing what should be built still requires understanding the people and problems involved.

articles.content:
Every month, the Chocolate Milk Cult reaches over a million Builders, Investors, Policy Makers, Leaders, and more. If you’d like to meet other members of our community, please fill out this contact form here (I will never sell your data nor will I make intros w/o your explicit permission)- https://forms.gle/Pi1pGLuS1FmzXoLr6
Databricks paid $1.3 billion for MosaicML. Harvey raised $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation. Gartner expects the specialized AI model market to reach $4.9 billion in 2026.
Several multi-billion dollar Silicon Valley backed companies are trying to sell you a similar philosophy: Your company has unique data. General AI doesn’t know that data. If you spend a fortune training on your own data, you can get much better returns compared to generic models.
Once you get into this cope, every road leads to becoming a training-cel. Have more data? Train more. Your information changes? Train again. The model still makes mistakes? Clearly, it needs more training. There is a loss function Shangri La after which all your business problems a prompt away from completion, and you should give joyfully give your AI Cloud providers all your operating margins to reach this happy ending.
However, there is a slight issue here… once you start getting into the details, a growing body of research suggests that training language models on proprietary knowledge is probably the most inefficient way to make that knowledge useful.
Now here you might stop and ask me about the impressive benchmark results. And how it makes intuitive sense that a model trained on the specific data/workflows will outperform general models. This is where we’re going to split training into two different outcomes —
Training to teach a model new facts is very expensive and mostly doesn’t work. We will go deep into the science of learning by exploring what pre-training, post-training, and continual learning can (and can’t) teach a model — and how much each approach will cost you.
Training to teach a model workflows (for eg how to navigate a filesystem to perform a certain task) is more grounded in science, but still doesn’t have the ROI that AI companies pretend it does.
Most importantly, I will show you with evidence how so many of the companies peddling this nonsense skip over the fact that many of the impressive improvements attributed to training can also come from building better reasoning, retrieval, memory and data infrastructure surrounding the model with more reliability and safety and at a much lower cost.
Now these are big claims, and I’m challenging some industry “best” practices (best for the investors and companies, for sure). I also understand that the people who peddle the post-training myth often struggle with reading the soo many big words that are found in research papers (which is why they are still peddling beliefs from the BERT era of LLMs). So in the spirit of good science and true intellectual inclusivity (literacy should not be a barrier to public participation), I am issuing a simple open challenge to anyone claiming the superiority of specialized training and can’t back it up by pointing to third party research (which doesn’t exist):
Use a real baseline. Compare your trained system against a capable model with proper reasoning, retrieval, memory, and tools. Beating a naked base model proves very little.
Show us your harness and evidence. Publish enough of your architecture, evaluations, and results to establish that training — not a weaker baseline — is responsible for the improvement.
Prove the economics. Compare the full cost of training against investing the same resources in better inference infrastructure. Include engineers, failed experiments, inference, refreshes, and vendor fees. Which investment delivers more?
Beat our general-purpose reasoning engine. We’ll compare your domain-trained system against Irys’s domain-agnostic reasoning infrastructure (you can sign up for a free Irys account in minutes, so there’s no setup complexity there; API also available) on identical inputs, with the same evaluation and transparent costs. Let’s see us what your specialization actually adds.
Join me as we do a Ateba Gautier level fraud-check on one of the most hyped trends in AI right now.
Pre-training is where models learn most of their factual knowledge. However this is extremely expensive, which is why most vendors use the language of pretraining (“train on your own data”, “models that remember your facts”) but in reality try to sell post training.
However, post-training is much better at teaching behaviors than reliably injecting new facts. So the mechanism they’re trying to sell doesn’t actually meet do what their marketing departments promise. While not the focus of this article, this is also why companies like Hippocratic AI, which imply that they have special ways to train domain specialized LLMs, are misleading customers. There just is no way to reliably inject knowledge in the weights of already trained LLMs.
This is clear when we look at the benchmark marketing. Vendors show impressive gains from training, but these amazing numbrs are often compared against weak baselines or unreproducable reasoning infrastructure. The latter is especially important when you consider that multiple bits of research have shown us that you can get really impressive results by improving the harness, w/ no investments in model training required.
This means that for most people investing in your own training pipeline (even the relatively cheaper post training) doesn’t manifest much ROI. This is especially true for systems that draft a lot (environments where files are changed constantly, tool specs are rebuilt etc). This drift is increasingly common with agentic systems (which tend to change a lot of things), hence we have seen the rise of continual learning. However…
Continual learning doesn’t magically solve the problem. Your knowledge, software, and workflows keep changing. Training-dependent improvements need ongoing updates and testing. Better retrieval, memory, and reasoning infrastructure can instead be reused across successive generations of models.
All in all, most of the conversation around training your models is smokes and mirrors that is meant for headlines but has almost no merit in actual research and products.

Which means you start again. And again. And again.

And again.

And again.

Until you and Totenham Fans are the only people left at the heat death of the universe, both waiting to reach the promised land that never came

Now compare that against spending the same money improving your retrieval, memory, and execution infrastructure. Better infrastructure can compound across generations of foundation models. When a stronger model arrives, you can plug it into the existing system and immediately benefit from the engineering you’ve already paid for. You maintain that infrastructure, of course, but you aren’t rebuilding specialized model weights every time the underlying technology advances.

To reiterate, training can absolutely improve performance. But that isn’t the question that people actually care about. The question is whether that improvement justifies the money, maintenance, and opportunity cost. And that answer is almost always a no, especially in the many non-tech domains where the solution is sold. Even Cursor, which has some major structural advantages — 

  • Operates in Coding, a more verifiable domain much closer to an AI researchers native domain expertise

  • Has a lot of money

  • Has a LOT of usage and traction.

  • Doesn’t have the AGI mandate and can focus on coding

still failed to push Composer to any meaningful difference compared to general models. So what secret do the other players in the space have?

This is a realization that most of the companies selling post training are slowly realizing. Which is why you’re seeing some goalposts being shifted, new terms being sold, and a whole new savior that will finally make domain specialized LLMs a reality.

Enter continous learning.

(Before I tear it apart, I want to differentiate between two things. As a researcher, I think CL is very interesting and has the potential to do some great things eventually. But for this article, our goal is to evaluate whether it’s ready to be sold in the short term, and that is a HELL NO).

3. Continual Learning: The Next Promised Land

The obvious problem with training models on company knowledge is that this knowledge keeps changing. Contracts get amended, regulations change, and workflows evolve. Constatly retraining models in the outdated ways is not sustainable. This is the impetus behind continual learning (CL): the field that studies how to keep updating the model with new information without destroying what it previously learned.

We would be very gung-ho about this field, except that updating knowledge is considerably harder than it sounds. A 2025 paper, The Mirage of Model Editing, found that knowledge-editing techniques reporting 96.8% success achieved just 38.5% under more realistic evaluations. Some earlier benchmarks had effectively leaked parts of the correct answers to models during testing. The methods also deteriorated dramatically after just 1,000 sequential edits.

And that’s before dealing with how corporate information actually works. Change a contract’s payment terms, and you’ve potentially changed its obligations, financial exposure, and everything that depends on those terms. Getting the model to remember the new number doesn’t mean it’ll update all the conclusions built on the old one.

A 2026 ACL study examined exactly this problem with evolving real-world knowledge. Continual fine-tuning, knowledge editing, and ordinary RAG all struggled with temporal consistency. The researchers improved results by organizing external evidence into a time-aware knowledge graph.

Notice what’s not needed? More training.

For the sake of argument, let’s say your vendor has the secret of continual learning (again a huge leap). Is there any utility to engaging with it then?

Each major refresh can mean preparing new training data, running experiments, evaluating what the model learned, checking what it forgot, and deploying another version. And you’re still paying the engineering team responsible for all of this. Let’s assume refreshing the model costs just 10% of the original $1.5 million GPU bill (this is really low if you look at the actual vendor claims, but we’re being generous here).

That’s $150,000 per update, or $1.8 million annually if you refresh monthly.

And you’re still quite susceptible to the generalization bias + environmental drift double whammy that hits normal training teams.

Compare that with maintaining knowledge externally. A contract changes? Update the record. A new regulation arrives? Update the knowledge base. Your reasoning system can access the latest information without another training cycle. Signals can be propogated more reliably (and most importantly you can detect every time they are not).

You still maintain and evaluate that infrastructure, but the investment can carry over to newer foundation models instead of remaining tied to one set of weights.

And once again, if any CL vendors have a problem with what I’m saying, let’s run a head to head publicly.

Conclusion: Don’t Train Your Own Model

There’s a rather beautiful business model hiding underneath all this. AI vendors get paid to train your models. Cloud providers get paid for the compute. Then everyone gets paid again when your data changes, your workflows evolve, or a better model comes along.

And somehow, you’re the one who’s supposed to be excited about this arrangement.

To reiterate what will undoubtely be deliberately misinterpreted about this article — I’m not saying that doesn’t work. I’m saying that for most (99%+) enterprise use cases, there are better and more efficient solutions out there. While commiting millions to your “own AI model” is a great way to get headlines and impress some board members, there’s honestly no good engineering or performance related reason to do so.

Your company’s knowledge doesn’t need to live inside a model’s weights. Your AI needs to know how to use it. That gets much easier with proper skills, documentation, and infra setup, especially as models get better with complex instruction following.

Perhaps we should try solving that problem before financing another GPU cluster.

“The fallacy is to believe that under a dictatorial government you can be free inside. Quite a number of people console themselves with this thought, now that totalitarianism in one form or another is visibly on the up-grade in every part of the world. Out in the street the loudspeakers bellow, the flags flutter from the rooftops, the police with their tommy-guns prowl to and fro, the face of the Leader, four feet wide, glares from every hoarding; but up in the attics the secret enemies of the régime can record their thoughts in perfect freedom — that is the idea, more or less. And many people are under the impression that this is going on now in Germany and other dictatorial countries.
Why is this idea false? I pass over the fact that modern dictatorships don’t, in fact, leave the loopholes that the old-fashioned despotisms did; and also the probable weakening of the desire for intellectual liberty owing to totalitarian methods of education. The greatest mistake is to imagine that the human being is an autonomous individual.”
—George Orwell, “As I Please”
I’ve been noticing a pattern in the United States and India, two countries that take up most of my time and attention. In the US, Flock’s network of over 120,000 cameras has sparked lawsuits and public backlash over mass surveillance and potential misuse. Here in India, the Delhi Police’s use of facial recognition to monitor protesters at Jantar Mantar has faced legal challenges of its own.
There are legitimate uses for these technologies, of course. But more often than not, new capabilities that come in with good intentions (but lacking the appropriate checks and balances) often become pillars for surveillance capitalism, institutional overreach, and totalitarian oppression. That makes it all the more important that people retain the ability to question, challenge, and resist abuses of that power. That’s all well and good, but the question is, how do we actually do that?
George Orwell is an obvious person to turn to here. He gets plenty of credit for anticipating surveillance, propaganda, and the machinery of authoritarian control. But in the same case as Harry Kane’s elite goalscoring drawing away attention from his also elite playmaking skills, I think people often overlook some of his most interesting insights; beyond explaining how institutions control people, Orwell also gives us something much more useful to think about: what makes people capable of resisting them in the first place?
To see what I mean, consider a rather odd detail at the end of 1984. The Party has already captured Winston and Julia. It knows everything about their affair, has extracted their confessions, and can imprison or execute them whenever it wants. Yet it goes to extraordinary lengths to make them genuinely betray one another, before eventually letting them go.
Why bother? What does destroying their relationship accomplish that all the Party’s surveillance, prisons, and torture couldn’t? That, my loves, is imo the real takeaway worth looking into from 1984.
Orwell’s most interesting warning goes beyond surveillance and propaganda. In 1984, the Party isn’t satisfied with controlling Winston and Julia; it needs them to betray each other. The point is to destroy loyalties and relationships that exist independently of the Party, leaving people with fewer ways to question or resist its authority.
Our understanding of reality is surprisingly dependent on other people. In Animal Farm, Napoleon abolishes debate and rewrites history, making it difficult for the animals to compare their experiences or organize against him. Several recognize that something is wrong, but individual skepticism is of little use when people cannot establish a common understanding and act together.
Relationships also develop the very abilities that make solidarity possible. Disagreements, compromises, rejection, and the general inconvenience of dealing with other people teach us to understand perspectives beyond our own. This matters politically because recognizing injustice is one thing; caring enough to inconvenience ourselves for somebody else is quite another.
AI introduces an interesting complication. We can increasingly get companionship, validation, and emotional support without much of that interpersonal friction. A study published in Science found that AI models affirmed users’ actions 49% more often than humans, while overly agreeable responses made people less willing to repair conflicts. Useful technology, certainly, but what happens if we gradually become less practised at navigating realities that don’t accommodate our own?
The political consequence is what interests me most. Surveillance becomes particularly dangerous when people lose the trust, shared reality, and willingness to stand up for one another that make resistance possible. I’m not arguing that AI companionship leads to totalitarianism. But while we’re busy worrying about institutions becoming powerful enough to watch everybody, it’s worth asking whether we’re becoming less capable of looking out for each other.

Everything else we shall destroy — everything…We have cut the links between child and parent, and between man and man, and between man and woman. No one dares trust a wife or a child or a friend any longer. But in the future there will be no wives and no friends. Children will be taken from their mothers at birth, as one takes eggs from a hen. The sex instinct will be eradicated. Procreation will be an annual formality like the renewal of a ration card. We shall abolish the orgasm. Our neurologists are at work upon it now. There will be no loyalty, except loyalty towards the Party. There will be no love, except the love of Big Brother. There will be no laughter, except the laugh of triumph over a defeated enemy. There will be no art, no literature, no science….Always, at every moment, there will be the thrill of victory, the sensation of trampling on an enemy who is helpless. If you want a picture of the future, imagine a boot stamping on a human face — for ever.”
— George Orwell, 1984
Let’s consider two things Orwell does across his most famous books.
1984: The Party already has Winston and Julia completely at its mercy, yet it goes to extraordinary lengths to make them betray each other. Why bother? Their relationship represents something the Party cannot control: an independent source of loyalty, trust, and shared experience. By destroying it, the Party undermines the very relationships through which people might question its authority.
Animal Farm: Napoleon achieves something similar by abolishing the animals’ meetings, rewriting their history, and making himself the authority through which they understand events. Several animals suspect something is wrong. Benjamin understands far more than most. But without the means to compare experiences and act together, their private understanding accomplishes remarkably little.
What interests me here is how much we rely on other people to understand the world. Friends expose us to experiences we haven’t had, colleagues help us recognize problems we thought were unique to us, and even ordinary conversations can challenge something we’ve believed for years. Through these interactions, we build a shared view of the world, a critical component for bringing together collaboration. Without that common ground, a population can contain plenty of intelligent, skeptical people who remain individually powerless.
“Napoleon, with the dogs following him, now mounted on to the raised portion of the floor where Major had previously stood to deliver his speech. He announced that from now on the Sunday-morning Meetings would come to an end. They were unnecessary, he said, and wasted time. In future all questions relating to the working of the farm would be settled by a special committee of pigs, presided over by himself. These would meet in private and afterwards communicate their decisions to the others. The animals would still assemble on Sunday mornings to salute the flag, sing Beasts of England, and receive their orders for the week; but there would be no more debates.
In spite of the shock that Snowball’s expulsion had given them, the animals were dismayed by this announcement. Several of them would have protested if they could have found the right arguments…Then the sheep broke out into a tremendous bleating of “Four legs good, two legs bad!” which went on for nearly a quarter of an hour and put an end to any chance of discussion.”
— George Orwell, Animal Farm, Chapter V
But relationships do something else that I think is equally important. The process of building them changes us.
Think about how many people you interact with before finding a handful of friends or somebody you love. You deal with disagreements, rejection, awkward conversations, and people whose priorities make absolutely no sense to you. Even the relationships that survive require work. You learn to accommodate other people’s needs, reconsider your judgments, and occasionally accept that someone else’s understanding of a situation is just as reasonable as yours. Not every interaction makes you a better person, obviously, but navigating other people’s realities is a large part of how we develop our own. And losing this will likely compromise something we haven’t adequately valued.
A study published in Science found that AI models affirmed users’ actions 49% more often than human respondents. Participants interacting with overly agreeable AI became more convinced they were right and less willing to repair interpersonal conflicts. They also preferred the agreeable responses. Even if one is careful about “sycophancy” and tries to share their situation with AI more objectively (and the AI itself is trying to be the best judge; very big assumption here), our own cognitive biases mean that we will fail to remember less flattering things and articulate the other party’s views properly.
Let’s play the implications of that out. What happens when we become accustomed to environments that adapt to our understanding of the world rather than requiring us to engage with somebody else’s? Much of our ability to recognize another person’s perspective develops through these encounters, including the inconvenient ones. Removing that friction may make companionship easier while leaving us less practised at dealing with people who aren’t like us. Ultimately, that takes away a key pillar of for us developing empathy, the capacity to care for another person, that might move us to bear discomfort for the sake of the other.
Now bring this into our earlier conversation about political consequences. Most people would be appalled at watching someone being unjustly dragged off the street. However, it’s much less striking to hear that an algorithm flagged someone and thus they were denied something essential. The consequences may be equally serious, but the latter is easier to experience as a statistical failure of the system rather than something happening to another person. If our social experiences increasingly revolve around individually tailored environments, what happens to our ability to recognize the lives affected by institutions operating far outside our immediate circles? What happens to our capacity to agree that we should care for them, that we should inconvenience ourselves for the ones beyond our noses on the faith that they would do the same for us?
“A British and a German historian would disagree deeply on many things, even on fundamentals, but there would still be that body of, as it were, neutral fact on which neither would seriously challenge the other. It is just this common basis of agreement, with its implication that human beings are all one species of animal, that totalitarianism destroys. Nazi theory indeed specifically denies that such a thing as ‘the truth’ exists. There is, for instance, no such thing as ‘science’. There is only ‘German science’, ‘Jewish science’ etc. The implied objective of this line of thought is a nightmare world in which the Leader, or some ruling clique, controls not only the future but the past. If the Leader says of such and such an event, ‘It never happened’ — well, it never happened. If he says that two and two are five — well, two and two are five. This prospect frightens me much more than bombs — and after our experiences of the last few years that is not a frivolous statement.”
— George Orwell, Looking Back on the Spanish War
Now it’s not my job (or interest) to shame you for relying on your very understanding AI Boyfriend to get the emotional support you need. Nor will I say that this is the path to you becoming a drone of totalitarianism, a worker grunt of the oligarchs. But I do think it is worth thinking about how the act might be stopping you from engaging with the world on your own terms, ultimately limiting your exposure to it. Because w/o, fighting for your freedom becomes an uphill battle.
“If there was hope, it must lie in the proles, because only there in those swarming disregarded masses, 85 per cent of the population of Oceania, could the force to destroy the Party ever be generated. The Party could not be overthrown from within. Its enemies, if it had any enemies, had no way of coming together or even of identifying one another. Even if the legendary Brotherhood existed, as just possibly it might, it was inconceivable that its members could ever assemble in larger numbers than twos and threes. Rebellion meant a look in the eyes, an inflexion of the voice, at the most, an occasional whispered word. But the proles, if only they could somehow become conscious of their own strength. would have no need to conspire. They needed only to rise up and shake themselves like a horse shaking off flies. If they chose they could blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning. Surely sooner or later it must occur to them to do it? And yet — !”
— George Orwell, 1984, Part One, Chapter VII
Coming back to the surveillance systems we discussed earlier, I think this is what makes Orwell particularly interesting. The problem isn’t simply whether a government can identify protesters or monitor its citizens. It’s also whether those citizens can recognize abuses, establish what happened, and find enough common ground to challenge them.
That requires more than information. Someone needs to care when a stranger is mistreated, believe their account, and sometimes accept personal inconvenience or risk to help them. Courts, journalists, civil liberties organizations, and ordinary communities all depend to some extent on people being willing and able to do this.
And that’s why I’m particularly interested in what we’re doing with our social lives. We can increasingly obtain companionship, validation, and personalized experiences without having to navigate much of the difficulty of understanding other people. Some of these technologies are genuinely helpful, but we’re not entirely sure what disappears when we remove the experiences that traditionally helped us develop those abilities.
“Actually, however, the avoidance of reality is much the same everywhere, and has much the same consequences. The Russian people were taught for years that they were better off than everybody else, and propaganda posters showed Russian families sitting down to abundant meal while the proletariat of other countries starved in the gutter. Meanwhile the workers in the western countries were so much better off than those of the U.S.S.R. that non-contact between Soviet citizens and outsiders had to be a guiding principle of policy…
To see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle.”
— George Orwell, In Front of Your Nose, 1946
I don’t think this means we’re heading toward 1984, nor that the inconvenience of other people is always worth preserving. But I do wonder whether our growing ability to make life comfortable within our own little worlds might leave us less equipped to understand the world outside them.
After all, much of what allows us to recognize injustice, particularly when it’s happening to somebody else, comes from the relationships and shared experiences through which we’ve learned to understand people beyond ourselves. And if those begin to disappear, I wonder how effectively we’ll be able to stand up for one another when it matters.
As a closing thought — we spend so much time discussing what happens when institutions become powerful enough to watch everybody. Orwell also makes me wonder what happens when the people being watched become less capable of trusting, understanding, or standing beside one another.

Their relationship represents something the Party cannot control: an independent source of loyalty, trust, and shared experience. By destroying it, the Party undermines the very relationships through which people might question its authority.

  • Animal Farm: Napoleon achieves something similar by abolishing the animals’ meetings, rewriting their history, and making himself the authority through which they understand events. Several animals suspect something is wrong. Benjamin understands far more than most. But without the means to compare experiences and act together, their private understanding accomplishes remarkably little.

What interests me here is how much we rely on other people to understand the world. Friends expose us to experiences we haven’t had, colleagues help us recognize problems we thought were unique to us, and even ordinary conversations can challenge something we’ve believed for years. Through these interactions, we build a shared view of the world, a critical component for bringing together collaboration. Without that common ground, a population can contain plenty of intelligent, skeptical people who remain individually powerless.

“Napoleon, with the dogs following him, now mounted on to the raised portion of the floor where Major had previously stood to deliver his speech. He announced that from now on the Sunday-morning Meetings would come to an end. They were unnecessary, he said, and wasted time. In future all questions relating to the working of the farm would be settled by a special committee of pigs, presided over by himself. These would meet in private and afterwards communicate their decisions to the others. The animals would still assemble on Sunday mornings to salute the flag, sing Beasts of England, and receive their orders for the week; but there would be no more debates.

In spite of the shock that Snowball’s expulsion had given them, the animals were dismayed by this announcement. Several of them would have protested if they could have found the right arguments…Then the sheep broke out into a tremendous bleating of “Four legs good, two legs bad!” which went on for nearly a quarter of an hour and put an end to any chance of discussion.”

— George Orwell, Animal Farm, Chapter V

But relationships do something else that I think is equally important. The process of building them changes us.

Think about how many people you interact with before finding a handful of friends or somebody you love. You deal with disagreements, rejection, awkward conversations, and people whose priorities make absolutely no sense to you. Even the relationships that survive require work. You learn to accommodate other people’s needs, reconsider your judgments, and occasionally accept that someone else’s understanding of a situation is just as reasonable as yours. Not every interaction makes you a better person, obviously, but navigating other people’s realities is a large part of how we develop our own. And losing this will likely compromise something we haven’t adequately valued.

A study published in Science found that AI models affirmed users’ actions 49% more often than human respondents. Participants interacting with overly agreeable AI became more convinced they were right and less willing to repair interpersonal conflicts. They also preferred the agreeable responses. Even if one is careful about “sycophancy” and tries to share their situation with AI more objectively (and the AI itself is trying to be the best judge; very big assumption here), our own cognitive biases mean that we will fail to remember less flattering things and articulate the other party’s views properly.

Let’s play the implications of that out. What happens when we become accustomed to environments that adapt to our understanding of the world rather than requiring us to engage with somebody else’s? Much of our ability to recognize another person’s perspective develops through these encounters, including the inconvenient ones. Removing that friction may make companionship easier while leaving us less practised at dealing with people who aren’t like us. Ultimately, that takes away a key pillar of for us developing empathy, the capacity to care for another person, that might move us to bear discomfort for the sake of the other.

Now bring this into our earlier conversation about political consequences. Most people would be appalled at watching someone being unjustly dragged off the street. However, it’s much less striking to hear that an algorithm flagged someone and thus they were denied something essential. The consequences may be equally serious, but the latter is easier to experience as a statistical failure of the system rather than something happening to another person. If our social experiences increasingly revolve around individually tailored environments, what happens to our ability to recognize the lives affected by institutions operating far outside our immediate circles? What happens to our capacity to agree that we should care for them, that we should inconvenience ourselves for the ones beyond our noses on the faith that they would do the same for us?

“A British and a German historian would disagree deeply on many things, even on fundamentals, but there would still be that body of, as it were, neutral fact on which neither would seriously challenge the other. It is just this common basis of agreement, with its implication that human beings are all one species of animal, that totalitarianism destroys. Nazi theory indeed specifically denies that such a thing as ‘the truth’ exists. There is, for instance, no such thing as ‘science’. There is only ‘German science’, ‘Jewish science’ etc. The implied objective of this line of thought is a nightmare world in which the Leader, or some ruling clique, controls not only the future but the past. If the Leader says of such and such an event, ‘It never happened’ — well, it never happened. If he says that two and two are five — well, two and two are five. This prospect frightens me much more than bombs — and after our experiences of the last few years that is not a frivolous statement.”

— George Orwell, Looking Back on the Spanish War

Now it’s not my job (or interest) to shame you for relying on your very understanding AI Boyfriend to get the emotional support you need. Nor will I say that this is the path to you becoming a drone of totalitarianism, a worker grunt of the oligarchs. But I do think it is worth thinking about how the act might be stopping you from engaging with the world on your own terms, ultimately limiting your exposure to it. Because w/o, fighting for your freedom becomes an uphill battle.

What Makes Resistance Possible?

“If there was hope, it must lie in the proles, because only there in those swarming disregarded masses, 85 per cent of the population of Oceania, could the force to destroy the Party ever be generated. The Party could not be overthrown from within. Its enemies, if it had any enemies, had no way of coming together or even of identifying one another. Even if the legendary Brotherhood existed, as just possibly it might, it was inconceivable that its members could ever assemble in larger numbers than twos and threes. Rebellion meant a look in the eyes, an inflexion of the voice, at the most, an occasional whispered word. But the proles, if only they could somehow become conscious of their own strength. would have no need to conspire. They needed only to rise up and shake themselves like a horse shaking off flies. If they chose they could blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning. Surely sooner or later it must occur to them to do it? And yet — !”

— George Orwell, 1984, Part One, Chapter VII

Coming back to the surveillance systems we discussed earlier, I think this is what makes Orwell particularly interesting. The problem isn’t simply whether a government can identify protesters or monitor its citizens. It’s also whether those citizens can recognize abuses, establish what happened, and find enough common ground to challenge them.

That requires more than information. Someone needs to care when a stranger is mistreated, believe their account, and sometimes accept personal inconvenience or risk to help them. Courts, journalists, civil liberties organizations, and ordinary communities all depend to some extent on people being willing and able to do this.

And that’s why I’m particularly interested in what we’re doing with our social lives. We can increasingly obtain companionship, validation, and personalized experiences without having to navigate much of the difficulty of understanding other people. Some of these technologies are genuinely helpful, but we’re not entirely sure what disappears when we remove the experiences that traditionally helped us develop those abilities.

“Actually, however, the avoidance of reality is much the same everywhere, and has much the same consequences. The Russian people were taught for years that they were better off than everybody else, and propaganda posters showed Russian families sitting down to abundant meal while the proletariat of other countries starved in the gutter. Meanwhile the workers in the western countries were so much better off than those of the U.S.S.R. that non-contact between Soviet citizens and outsiders had to be a guiding principle of policy…

To see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle.”

— George Orwell, In Front of Your Nose, 1946

I don’t think this means we’re heading toward 1984, nor that the inconvenience of other people is always worth preserving. But I do wonder whether our growing ability to make life comfortable within our own little worlds might leave us less equipped to understand the world outside them.

After all, much of what allows us to recognize injustice, particularly when it’s happening to somebody else, comes from the relationships and shared experiences through which we’ve learned to understand people beyond ourselves. And if those begin to disappear, I wonder how effectively we’ll be able to stand up for one another when it matters.

As a closing thought — we spend so much time discussing what happens when institutions become powerful enough to watch everybody. Orwell also makes me wonder what happens when the people being watched become less capable of trusting, understanding, or standing beside one another.
